Korea Times: "The South Korean surplus totaled $49.73 billion in June, up from the previous record of $38.61 billion in May."

These are incredibly large surpluses. This is why I have long argued that the problem isn't China. It is a global trading system that allows, and even rewards, countries that choose to suppress domestic demand in order to make their manufacturing sectors more competitive than those of their trading partners.

It does this by allowing them with no penalty to run the trade surpluses that force their trade partners to absorb the costs of their domestic policies. This is precisely what Keynes argued against at Bretton Woods.
https://t.co/OOej62gK1K

They probably save so much because of high unemployment and underemployment, stagnant and even declining wages in many parts of the economy, rising job uncertainty, especially among the young, aging populations, and so on. You can see this in gold and jewelry purchases. Purchases of gold bars and coins are soaring, even as purchases of jewelry are plummeting.

There are potential government policies that can shift household behavior from saving to consumption, like putting in place better unemployment and pension benefits, etc. but previous attempts suggest there is little credibility, and it might take years, or even decades, before a better social safety net will change saving patterns significantly.

This is the classic problem of rebalancing under excessive debt. As the fiscal space tightens, China urgently needs to increase fiscal revenues, but doing so means either squeezing businesses, which is bad for growth, or squeezing households, which is bad for rebalancing.

The "reward" for harder work should be higher wages, not higher surpluses. Higher surpluses simply mean that businesses and the very rich capture a higher share of production than among its trade partners, and workers a lower share, whether or not the country indeed "works harder".

Ten years ago, when German wages were much lower relative to German productive, everyone (including the Germans themselves) spoke about how disciplined and thrifty Germans are. Today, as wage growth has caught up to productivity growth, we have suddenly discovered that Germans are in fact lazy and spendthrift.

This is just a very lazy way of understanding the economy. A country is not a household. And, contrary to the popular misconception,  a country's "income" is not its trade balance. It is absurd to argue that the bigger a country's trade surplus, the more it is earning and so the harder it is working. 

A country's income in fact is the total value of its domestic production. The more it produces, the more it should consume, but the less it consumes, the greater its trade surplus.

The AST6200 is China's first domestic front-end lithography tool to enter production. I don't mean to downplay it because they are competing against decades-old established players in the lithography world, ASML, Canon, Nikon, and others. But the reality here is this new tool will compete against ASML's refurbished tool market. The specification falls somewhere between the 275D and 100D from the 1990s.

To the right is ASML's latest i-line tool, the 400M. This is a new productivity upgrade on the 400L system. When you compare the performance differences, it's obvious why ASML discontinued the older platform; it just doesn't work for a 300 mm fab. The big market for i-line now is a screaming fast 300 mm system like this one. The throughput of this system has in fact triggered a lot of photoresist qualifications because many legacy resists can not meet the speed requirements for the newer tool.

A new player in the 200mm i-line market will face a lot of uphill battles. The new installs for this are mainly relegated to compound semi where the wafer size is still 200mm or smaller.
